GhostAction hijacked about 1,900 GitHub accounts to plant credential-stealing Actions workflows in 30,000 repos. Blocking them won’t secure your secrets.

item.title: Vercel adds always-on workers to run more of your backend
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
Vercel is giving developers more options for running their backends on its platform. At its Ship conference in San Francisco

The post Vercel adds always-on workers to run more of your backend appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Vercel is giving developers more options for running their backends on its platform.

At its Ship conference in San Francisco on Thursday, the company introduced Daemons, a new service for continuously running background workers, and made its Python support generally available.

It also made Drives, its persistent storage for AI agents, generally available.

Always-on workers, pull-based jobs

Daemons, which is now in public beta, lets developers deploy a container and specify how many instances should run in each region. Vercel makes sure those processes keep running and restarts them if they exit or crash. At launch, it supports pull-based workloads that allow workers to fetch jobs from a queue or database and then process them as they arrive.

Vercel CTO Malte Ubl tells The New Stack that the company’s current push in terms of going further down the stack.

“Let’s look at what people are doing, and let’s make sure that a larger chunk of them could just only use Vercel as their infrastructure provider,” he says.

The company already offers queues and durable workflows, while its Services feature lets developers deploy frontends and backends together.

These features cover request-driven work, Ubl says, but not everything a sophisticated backend does. “What really doesn’t fit well into that bucket is what you do find in sophisticated backend workloads,” he says, “where you want to do essentially processing on some kind of queue,” he says.

He uses Vercel’s own deployment pipeline as an example for that kind of workload.

“When you call our API to make a deployment, we don’t do that deployment in that process that handles your request, because we can’t actually do an infinite number of concurrent deployments,” Ubl says. GitHub rate limits are one reason to back off, and Vercel’s existing compute primitives didn’t give developers “good control over the amount of concurrency” for that kind of worker.

With Daemons, “they come up, they start saying, here I am, give me work, and then they just process as it goes,” he says.

The company’s example for using Daemons combines a Next.js frontend with a Python API, as well as a containerized video processor. The container packages Python dependencies and the FFmpeg media framework, and then pulls jobs from Vercel Queues to generate playback files and thumbnails.

Transcoding is a typical case, Ubl says, with “extremely CPU-bound workloads” where “I just need computers that I want to always be 100% CPU.”

That also puts Daemons at the opposite end of the spectrum from Vercel’s sandboxes. “They’re almost the opposite of temporary,” he says of Daemons. “For temporary, you have sandboxes,” he says. Daemons stay on but aren’t invoked by requests from the internet. They reach out for work instead.

Developers can deploy through Git or the Vercel CLI. Vercel builds the container image and stores it in its Container Registry.

The company itself runs a good chunk of its control plane API on Vercel. That accounts for about a billion requests a month, Ubl says, and Vercel is now starting to move many of its asynchronous workloads onto Daemons.

Vercel didn’t invent the model, he acknowledges, “we ship it because people very much want this.”

Managed runtime or container

If you’re deep in the Vercel ecosystem, you may wonder how all of this relates to Vercel Functions.

Vercel says 5,000 teams have made 150,000 container deployments since container support entered public beta. Containers let developers package applications with their own runtimes and system libraries, expanding the range of software they can deploy.

The trade-off here is who keeps the image current, Uble argues. With a managed runtime for Node, Bun, or Python, Vercel applies a security release without the customer redeploying, Ubl says. With a container, “you do have to redeploy. It’s ultimately your responsibility,” he says. “From our point of view, it’s just bytes.”

Python support, meanwhile, is now generally available for frameworks including FastAPI, Flask, and Django. Applications run on standard CPython with PyPI dependencies, while Vercel handles framework detection, builds, and scaling. The company says 150,000 teams already run Python backends on its platform, including engineers at OpenAI, Polymarket, and Exa.

Files that survive a change of environment

Vercel Drives is a great example of how agents are changing the requirements for backend services like storage. Vercel’s Drives service separates an agent’s files from the sandbox executing its code. An agent can mount the drive in a new sandbox, change runtimes, and continue working with the files it already created.

“I wouldn’t claim it’s an industry first, but it’s certainly an instance of a new type of storage product,” Ubl says. He describes it as a hybrid of an EBS-style networked drive and object storage, something he doesn’t think AWS offers.

Writes always land on local NVMe disk and stream asynchronously to object storage, he says, and reads come from the local disk when the data is already there — or stream in block by block.

“You have a very large number of independent disks, which, because they’re just files in S3, are arbitrarily cheap to operate,” he says.

Drives versus snapshots

Many sandbox providers, Vercel included, offer snapshots, Ubl says, but he argues drives are the better model.

“The problem with snapshots is they get really big, because you ultimately snapshot all kinds of stuff that is the same every time,” he says. “In practice, what agents really do is there’s some directory, I don’t know, /home/agent. That’s where everything is. Everything else they don’t really care about.”

Mounting that one directory means every agent can boot from the same cached base image, he says. “It’s cheaper for them, it’s faster. There’s essentially no downside.”

Vercel isn’t removing snapshots, Ubl adds, but it is encouraging customers to switch.

Drives lets those agents reuse each other’s work. One can prepare a dataset while others mount read-only copies to analyze it or generate reports, saving their results separately. Agents can also fork a drive to test different approaches in independent writable workspaces. Those forks don’t merge back into the original.

In practice, Ubl says, that means telling the agent where to write. “When you use a sandbox, you always tell your agent where it should write things,” he says, typically a root directory such as /workspace. “Essentially every prompt will start with that sentence, and then that’s just what you mount into your durable drive, and that’s it.”

Drives and forking are generally available. The service is available on all Vercel plans, with default capacities of 1 TiB, or 1 GiB on Hobby, and configurations up to 16 TiB.

For a team already deploying its frontend on Vercel, running a worker or Python API there becomes an easier decision. Each additional backend service it can keep on the platform is one fewer deployment system its developers have to maintain.

The post Vercel adds always-on workers to run more of your backend appeared first on The New Stack.
Vercel adds Daemons, always-on background workers, plus persistent Drives for AI agents and GA Python support, as it pushes deeper into backend hosting.

item.title: OpenAI promised developers six months’ notice. GPT-4o users got three.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
OpenAI is retiring four GPT-4 models from its API on January 14, 2027. The deprecation notice the company sent developers

The post OpenAI promised developers six months’ notice. GPT-4o users got three. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI is retiring four GPT-4 models from its API on January 14, 2027. The deprecation notice the company sent developers Wednesday covers GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, GPT-4.1, and GPT-4.1 mini, along with their dated snapshots and every fine-tuned model built on top of them.

With just three months to migrate production traffic, OpenAI’s recommended replacement, GPT-6 Luna, handles reasoning and tool calls differently enough that swapping the model ID may be the easiest part of the migration.

With just three months to migrate production traffic, OpenAI’s recommended replacement, GPT-6 Luna, handles reasoning and tool calls differently enough that swapping the model ID may be the easiest part of the migration.

GPT-4o’s long goodbye

GPT-4o arrived on May 13, 2024, as OpenAI’s flagship and built a following loyal enough to change the company’s plans. When GPT-5 replaced it in August 2025, Reddit filled with complaints, and OpenAI brought it back for paying ChatGPT subscribers the very next day. That reprieve lasted until February 13, 2026, when GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 disappeared from ChatGPT. Both remained available through the API, but that access now is sunsetting.

By then, OpenAI said just 0.1% of daily ChatGPT users were still choosing GPT-4o, although the model continued serving API requests for applications built around it.

GPT-4.1 was a different kind of release, arriving on April 14, 2025, as an API-only family that skipped ChatGPT entirely and went straight after developers with stronger coding, better instruction following, room for up to a million tokens of context, and more reliable diff formats for anyone letting a model loose on large files.

Kevin Weil, OpenAI’s chief product officer, called them models “trained just for developers” during the launch livestream, and Sam Altman went on X to say developers “seem very happy” with them.

Luna pricing has fine print

Luna is the fastest and cheapest tier of GPT-6, and on paper it covers the basics GPT-4.1 offered, with a 1.05 million-token context window, structured outputs and function calling. At $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, it’s cheaper than GPT-5.6 Luna, which charged twice as much for input and $1.20 per million output tokens.

Once a prompt passes 272,000 input tokens, the input rate doubles the output rate raises by 50% for the entire request. That could eat into the savings for RAG pipelines and coding agents working with large codebases.

OpenAI’s migration guide says GPT-6 Luna defaults to medium reasoning effort but supports function calling through Chat Completions only with reasoning_effort=none. Combining reasoning and tool calls requires the Responses API. Enabling reasoning also rules out temperature, top_p, top_logprobs, and logprobs, all supported by GPT-4.1.

The company recommends using its Docs skill in Codex to update API calls across a project, but those changes won’t account for differences in model behavior. Anthropic ran into a similar problem last month when Opus 5.5 introduced four breaking changes, causing 400 errors in existing agent integrations. Other changes altered how agents behaved without triggering errors, making those regressions harder to catch.

No fine-tuning on Luna

New self-serve fine-tuning jobs end on January 6, 2027, eight days before the GPT-4 models retire. Existing fine-tuned models will continue serving inference requests until January 14, leaving a short window to run replacements alongside them.

New self-serve fine-tuning jobs end on January 6, 2027, eight days before the GPT-4 models retire.

Six months’ notice, three delivered

Other deadlines are on OpenAI’s deprecation schedule, which includes GPT-4.1 nano, the first GPT-4o snapshot, and older GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and o-series models retiring October 23. GPT-5 and o3 snapshots follow December 11, with selected legacy audio, real-time, and transcription models scheduled for January 20, 2027. GPT-5.1, GPT-5.3-Codex and GPT-5.4-Nano are set to retire April 1.

The List models API now includes a shutdown_date field, making it possible to check upcoming retirements automatically. Customers who need more time may be able to keep older models running through dedicated capacity, although they’ll have to arrange that with OpenAI’s sales team.

The three-month warning also falls short of OpenAI’s own deprecation policy, which promises at least six months’ notice for generally available models. The policy allows exceptions for safety or compliance reasons, but there’s no explanation for why GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 are getting only half that time.

The three-month warning also falls short of OpenAI’s own deprecation policy, which promises at least six months’ notice for generally available models.

The post OpenAI promised developers six months’ notice. GPT-4o users got three. appeared first on The New Stack.
OpenAI will shut off GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 API access in January. Moving to GPT-6 Luna changes tool calls, pricing for long prompts and fine-tuned models.

item.title: Meta ships Muse Spark Open, its answer to China’s best open-weight models
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
Meta on Thursday launched Muse Spark Open, a new 816B open model (with 42B active parameters) that the company argues

The post Meta ships Muse Spark Open, its answer to China’s best open-weight models appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Meta on Thursday launched Muse Spark Open, a new 816B open model (with 42B active parameters) that the company argues is the “most capable US open-weight model to date.”

The new model is available through the APIs of Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter, and Together AI. And since it’s an open model, you can also download the weights from Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden, Hugging Face, and Microsoft’s Foundry Model Catalog.

Open Weights, semi-open license

Overall, Muse Spark Open, which features the industry-standard 1 million token window, looks to be an extremely capable model that, depending on the benchmark, is on par with or beats some of the best Chinese models. Like with some of the newer Chinese models, though, the weights may be open but the license doesn’t tell the same story.

Meta is launching the new model under the “Muse Model License.” This license, Meta says, has “limited commercial terms, which allow many developers to use the model for free.”

Specifically, this means any company that has more than $20 million in gross revenue during any consecutive twelve-month period must “notify Meta and enter into a separate written agreement with Meta before offering the Software or any Derivatives as part of that Model as a Service business.”

Any company using the model must also “prominently display ‘Built with Muse Spark Open’ in the user interface of each product or service” that uses the model or a derivative model that was created, trained, fine-tuned, or distilled from Muse Spark Open.

Overall, this looks a lot like the license that Moonshot uses for Kimi K3, for example.

Internal use and building the model into your own product are free, and the license’s usage policy bars military and critical infrastructure deployments, a carve-out Meta added for the U.S. government with Llama in 2024.

Unlike Anthropic’s new usage policy for Claude, though, you can abuse the model as much as you want.

Benchmarks

The company says it built the new model for “coding and agentic work, it excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning.”

The two U.S. models Muse Spark Open competes with are essentially Thinking Machines’ Inkling and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3 Ultra. In Meta’s own benchmarks, its new model beats them across the board — often by 20 points or more.

The closer fight, however, is with Chinese open models that many developers already run today. Spark Open leads Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, and Qwen3.8 on the agentic and tool-use benchmarks, including JobBench and MCP-Atlas, and roughly ties them on SciCode.

Coding is where it trails.

On Terminal-Bench 2.1, Kimi K3 scores 85.0 and GLM 5.3 83.9 against Spark Open’s 76.4.

On DeepSWE 1.1, the spread is 68 to 60. That’s the same gap Meta acknowledged when it launched the closed version of Spark in April, and it doesn’t look like it’s made much progress since.

Muse Spark Open on the Mac you can’t afford

You’re unlikely to run an 816B model locally, but if you have two new Mac Studios with M5 Ultra chips and 512 GB, Meta says you could link them and use MLX to run the model on them.

The company did just that to run Muse Code, powered by Muse Spark, and ship updates to the Ice Cubes Mastodon client, for example. Apple doesn’t currently sell the 512 GB Mac Studio to mere mortals, but in a few weeks, you will be able to buy two of those machines for the price of a compact car.

The post Meta ships Muse Spark Open, its answer to China’s best open-weight models appeared first on The New Stack.
Meta’s Muse Spark Open is an 816B open-weight model that beats US rivals and matches Chinese models on agentic tasks, but its license isn’t fully open.

item.title: Nvidia squeezed a 74B agent model into 24GB so it can run on your laptop
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
Nvidia on Thursday announced a few new additions to its Nemotron family: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B vision-language model for

The post Nvidia squeezed a 74B agent model into 24GB so it can run on your laptop appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia on Thursday announced a few new additions to its Nemotron family: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B vision-language model for enterprise agents and two small Bolt models (Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB) for running coding, research, and conversational workloads locally.

The Bolt models, Nvidia says, are meant to run “everyday agentic tasks on laptops, balancing speed and intelligence needed to handle multistep reasoning, tool calling, and web browsing.”

And while they come in very different sizes and are meant for different use cases, the focus for all three is on speed and efficiency.

The two larger models are available today, while the smaller Bolt E4B 4G model will launch in the near future.

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL

The marquee release here is Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120-billion-parameter model that combines reasoning and tool use with image and document understanding.

In the announcement, Kari Briski, Nvidia’s VP for open models and software, notes that the large model is meant to deliver “leading accuracy on multimodal agentic tasks — instruction following, tool use, multistep business workflows, and visual understanding — comparable with NVIDIA’s largest reasoning model at roughly one-fifth the parameter count.”

Super VL builds on Nemotron 3 Super, which launched in March. Both have 120 billion total parameters, with 12 billion active during inference, and context windows of up to 1 million tokens. But while the earlier model only accepted text, Super VL now adds support for image and video input (though not output).

Mixed results against Qwen

But when it comes to the benchmarks, though, especially when compared to other open models of comparable size, the results are mixed.

In Nvidia’s own evaluations, Super VL outperforms Alibaba’s Qwen3.5-122B-A10B on scientific reasoning and terminal tasks, while scoring slightly lower on SWE-bench Verified and document understanding.

The five tests are GPQA-Diamond, Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-bench Verified, IFBench, and MMLongBench-Doc. Super VL scores 66.7 on Terminal-Bench, compared with Qwen3.5’s 48.7, but trails it on SWE-bench Verified, 71.1 to 71.9.

Qwen has 122 billion total parameters and 10 billion active, compared with Super VL’s 120 billion and 12 billion. The newer Qwen3.8-Flash-Next scores higher on all five tests, though its additional embedding and prediction components bring its total parameter count to about 180 billion.

Thinking Machines’ Inkling-Small has 276 billion total parameters and 12 billion active. It also trails Super VL on terminal tasks but scores higher on instruction following.

Nvidia also reports Super VL ahead of Ultra on Hermes Bench and LangChain behavioral evaluations, scoring 63.44% versus 56.33% and 87.05% versus 84.3%, respectively.

Overall, though, the focus here was clearly on speed.

Nvidia reports fourfold faster completion of 10,000 SWE-bench Pro tasks on four B200 GPUs, though its chart shows lower accuracy than Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and DeepSeek V4 Flash.

Hybrid Mamba architecture, faster decoding

As for how Nvidia built the model, it’s worth noting that the Nemotron coalition is sticking to the 3.5 family’s hybrid architecture, which combines Mamba-2, attention, and mixture-of-experts layers — but with the addition of a vision encoder. Nvidia also continued training the language model using distillation from Nemotron 3 Ultra before further training for software engineering, vision, and agent tasks, according to its model card.

To speed up text generation, Nvidia also uses LiLiCorr, a technique for speculative decoding. With this, a smaller helper model drafts several tokens ahead, which Super VL checks together instead of generating each token individually. Nvidia says this speeds up token generation on DGX Spark by up to 2.3 times compared with decoding without speculation.

For document workflows, Nvidia says Super VL focuses on optical character recognition, tables, charts, and structured information.

On CharXiv, a chart-reasoning benchmark, Nvidia reports 80.8% accuracy, compared with Nano Omni’s 63%. Python code interpretation raises Super VL’s result to 84%.

Bolt runs 74B in 24GB

If you’re interested in running local models, the new Bolt models may be the most interesting release here — and their benchmarks tend to outperform most comparable models.

Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is derived from Super VL. Its hybrid mixture-of-experts architecture activates 9 billion of its 74 billion parameters at a time.

In Nvidia’s tests, Bolt scores 51.0 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, versus 44.4 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and 37.2 for Gemma4 26B-A4B, both tested in BF16. Bolt uses mixed precision, including two-bit experts.

To get to this size, Nvidia used two-bit quantization to reduce the 74B model’s memory footprint to 24GB. The company says it is optimizing the model for RTX Spark and DGX Spark systems, with support for llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, and vLLM.

A second, even smaller version of this model, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, is scheduled for later this month. With this one, Nvidia is targeting conversational and physical agents on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and Spark hardware, including device assistants and interactive characters that need multiturn tool use and awareness of application state.

Availability

The new models are now available for download on Hugging Face under the OpenMDW 1.1 license, which permits commercial use and modification.

The post Nvidia squeezed a 74B agent model into 24GB so it can run on your laptop appeared first on The New Stack.
Nemotron 3.5 Bolt uses 2-bit quantization to fit a 74B mixture-of-experts model in 24GB, and Nvidia says it still beats Qwen and Gemma on agent benchmarks.

item.title: What it takes to become an AI company: Four lessons from the top
item.dc:creator: Walid Abu-Hadba
item.description:
Every company is under pressure to become “an AI company.” Over the past several months, we’ve been undertaking that transformation

The post What it takes to become an AI company: Four lessons from the top appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Every company is under pressure to become “an AI company.” Over the past several months, we’ve been undertaking that transformation at Precisely, changing how we build, work, and measure progress.

That experience has reinforced something for me: the hardest parts of becoming an AI company have relatively little to do with the technology.

AI can help an organization move faster, automate work, increase capacity, and fundamentally change what people can accomplish. But none of those things guarantees better business performance.

“The hardest parts of becoming an AI company have relatively little to do with the technology.”

Four leadership lessons have emerged from that experience:

  1. Start with the business objective
  2. Simplify before accelerating
  3. Redesign how people work
  4. Measure the results that matter

Start with the business objective

First, clarify what the business is trying to achieve. That needs to be a business outcome: growth, faster innovation, stronger customer relationships, better products, improved margins, or something else that matters to the strategy.

AI dramatically expands what is possible. That makes focus critically important. Leaders must establish clear priorities: what needs to improve, what the organization needs to start doing, and just as importantly, what it needs to stop doing.

That clarity filters where to invest, which processes to change, and where AI can create the most value.

Without it, AI can proliferate complexity rather than reduce it. Organizations deploy more tools, launch more agents, and generate more activity without a clear connection to the business outcome they are trying to achieve.

That’s why I think of AI as an operating model, not a strategy. Strategy establishes where the business is going and why. AI can change how quickly and effectively you get there.

Simplify before you accelerate

Once the objective is clear, leaders need to examine how work gets done.

AI can make almost anything move faster. That’s both the opportunity and the problem.

Apply AI to a process that no longer adds value, and you’ve simply made a bad process run faster. Automate one step while leaving the same unnecessary approvals, handoffs, meetings, and decision points around it, and the bottleneck moves from one point to another.

“Apply AI to a process that no longer adds value, and you’ve simply made a bad process run faster.”

I’ve seen this firsthand. As AI accelerates areas like software development, constraints often shift to the processes around the work. If an engineer can generate code 4x faster, but that code still waits in the same queues and moves through the same handoffs, the organization hasn’t created 4x the value.

The entire system has to evolve.

The principle is straightforward:

Eliminate what doesn’t add value à Simplify what does à Then use AI to accelerate it

Redesign how people work

Technology alone doesn’t transform an organization. People have to change how they work.

I saw this in an unexpected place at Precisely: our summer intern program.

Our interns arrived with different levels of AI experience and different ideas about what it might mean for their careers. Over ten weeks, I watched those perceptions change. Once they could apply AI to real work, they moved faster, explored challenges more deeply, and became more confident in what they could accomplish.

What struck me most was how quickly their sense of what they were capable of changed, and how contagious that confidence became.

That experience reinforced something I believe leaders need to understand about AI: the baseline for what people can accomplish is changing. And this extends well beyond people entering the workforce.

As AI takes on more execution and routine work, people at every level have greater capacity to set direction, evaluate outputs, solve difficult problems, build relationships, and apply judgment and expertise.

“Giving employees access to AI and measuring usage will only take an organization so far. Leaders need to examine how the work itself should change.”

That has significant implications for how leaders think about jobs, skills, and development. The assumptions we have built around what a role looks like, how long it takes someone to become proficient, and what people at different career stages can contribute will have to evolve.

Workflows need to evolve, too. Giving employees access to AI and measuring usage will only take an organization so far. Leaders need to examine how the work itself should change: where AI belongs in the process, what it can take on, where human judgment remains essential, and what people can now accomplish with the capacity AI creates.

Our interns gave me an early glimpse of what that can look like. The leadership challenge is creating the conditions for that same shift to happen across the organization.

Measure what the business gets back

Finally, leaders need to be disciplined about measuring progress.

At some point, AI adoption became a business metric. Organizations track how many employees are using AI, how many agents they’ve deployed, or how many tokens they process.

Those numbers can tell you whether people are using AI. They can’t tell you whether AI is creating value.

We never measured the ROI of email. We didn’t track spreadsheet adoption or ask for weekly reports on how many documents were created in Word. We treated them as infrastructure and measured what the business did with them.

Adoption is an input, not an outcome.

Productivity should create capacity. That capacity should let teams move faster, bring ideas to market sooner, spend more time on work that requires judgment and expertise, and create better customer experiences. Those gains then need to translate into growth and stronger business performance.

“Adoption is an input, not an outcome. The greater opportunity is expanding what an organization can accomplish with the people and expertise it already has.”

That’s why I believe leaders should see AI as an opportunity to do more with the same, not as an opportunity to do more with less.

If your AI strategy focuses on headcount reduction, you’re treating AI as an efficiency tool. That can reduce costs in the short term, but it doesn’t provide long-term value. The greater opportunity is expanding what an organization can accomplish with the people and expertise it already has.

The leadership challenge ahead

I’m optimistic about what AI will mean for work.

Technology has always changed what people do and raised the ceiling on what they can accomplish. AI is accelerating that pattern.

But simply having the technology won’t create competitive advantage.

The differentiator will be how organizations use it.

That means staying focused on the business objective, eliminating complexity before accelerating it, redesigning work around what people and AI can accomplish together, and holding the transformation accountable to business results.

The true measure of AI is what your business can now do that it couldn’t do before.

The post What it takes to become an AI company: Four lessons from the top appeared first on The New Stack.
Becoming an AI company isn't about technology. Here are four leadership lessons on simplifying work and driving true business value.

item.title: Anthropic’s been eyeing confidential AI. It just made its move with another acquihire.
item.dc:creator: Meredith Shubel
item.description:
Anthropic’s done it again. On Tuesday, Opaque Systems announced a new agreement with Anthropic that “carries Opaque’s work forward.”  Vague

The post Anthropic’s been eyeing confidential AI. It just made its move with another acquihire. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic’s done it again. On Tuesday, Opaque Systems announced a new agreement with Anthropic that “carries Opaque’s work forward.” 

Vague wording aside, the agreement marks another acquihire for Anthropic, with the AI juggernaut licensing Opaque’s technology and bringing on board some (but not all) of its employees, including Opaque CEO Aaron Fulkerson and CTO Rishabh Poddar, reports The Information.

The agreement gives Anthropic access to expertise in confidential AI, the “real-world technology” and category Opaque claims it helped define after starting as a research project at UC Berkeley’s RISELab 10 years ago with the goal to “enabl[e] organizations to use their most sensitive data while keeping it private, even while it’s being used.”

For now, both Anthropic and Opaque are pretty mum on the details of the deal, leaving one obvious question on everyone’s mind:

What will happen to Opaque’s open-source ecosystem? And what does that mean for the developers relying on them?

What is confidential AI? And what does Opaque bring to the table? 

On LinkedIn, where he shared news of the agreement, Fulkerson reflected on Opaque’s work defining the category of confidential AI, what he described as “verifiability for the AI stack.” 

When asked for more information on the term, Arjun Jaggi, associate director of R&D innovation at Cognizant, describes confidential computing in AI to The New Stack as “running workloads on sensitive data while the data stays protected by the hardware itself, even while it’s being used.”

Whether or not it truly defined the category, the startup’s sure been making its mark. Earlier this year, it closed a $24 million Series B with a $300 million valuation. It’s also spearheaded a slew of industry initiatives. 

It created the Confidential Computing Summit, an event Fulkerson says it has now handed over to the Linux Foundation, which already co-hosted this year’s June summit with Opaque. Working with the UAE’s Technology Innovation Institute, it created an open standard for verifiable AI governance. In June this year, it launched AgenTrust, an open-source community for verifiable agent governance, and Confidential MCP, which Opaque bills as the first verifiably governed, secure MCP implementation.

Now, as Opaque enters into a deal with one of the biggest names in the AI space, the obvious question is what will happen to the technology and community it helped build. So far, reactions are mixed. 

Anthropic’s been transparent about its interest in confidential AI

In 2024, Jason Clinton, Anthropic’s chief information security officer, appeared on Opaque’s AI Confidential podcast, where he discussed the importance of confidential computing for the future of AI. Afterward, Fulkerson recapped the conversation with a post, the title of which made clear Anthropic’s confidential AI aspirations: “The Mathematical Case for Trusted AI: Why Anthropic is All-In on Confidential Computing.”

Then in 2025, Anthropic published research with Pattern Labs on confidential inference, an approach to protecting sensitive data and AI model weights: “Confidential Inference via Trusted Virtual Machines.” The AI company acknowledged the work was still preliminary, calling it “just a sketch of our research” that was “still early.”

And by early 2026, Anthropic was named in Opaque’s list of customers and partners.

“When a frontier lab like Anthropic takes a promising confidential computing tool and puts real resources behind it, that’s often how a research stage project becomes something hardened enough for production — and an under-funded startup might never get it there on its own.” 

Looking back, those public statements suggest Anthropic has been thinking about confidential AI well before its Opaque deal. Whether the new agreement will benefit the industry as a whole, though, remains unknown. 

Jaggi, at least, is taking an optimistic stance, telling The New Stack Anthropic’s resources could give the technology the push it needs to grow: 

“I’d actually frame this more positively than most. When a frontier lab like Anthropic takes a promising confidential computing tool and puts real resources behind it, that’s often how a research stage project becomes something hardened enough for production — and an under-funded startup might never get it there on its own.” 

Others are more skeptical, though.

When asked for his take, Michael Heinrich, co-founder and CEO of 0G Labs, tells The New Stack he sees the agreement as a good move for Anthropic, which can piggyback on Opaque’s decade of confidential computing research. What he expresses caution about is a potential conflict of interest:

“The whole point of confidential computing is that you don’t have to trust the operator. When the tools that produce that proof sit inside a model vendor, the party being checked now owns part of the checking.” 

Both are opaque on the details of the deal

In his LinkedIn post, Fulkerson describes his move to Anthropic as a natural fit, writing, “Their culture, their mission and their values align with mine, personally and professionally.” 

In its announcement, Opaque itself is similarly vague, calling the agreement a “next chapter” that “carries Opaque’s work forward.” 

Anthropic, for its part, has told The Information that it’s licensing Opaque’s technology and hiring some of its engineers but has otherwise released no further information. 

“The whole point of confidential computing is that you don’t have to trust the operator. When the tools that produce that proof sit inside a model vendor, the party being checked now owns part of the checking.” 

So the (unanswered) elephant in the room is: What happens to all of Opaque’s existing initiatives? The governance framework? AgenTrust? Confidential MCP? 

We know that Opaque has passed its summit to the Linux Foundation. But questions remain about the startup’s open-source projects, as neither Opaque nor Anthropic has made any statements about maintenance commitments. 

Heinrich seems relatively unconcerned for now, telling TNS that Confidential MCP is MIT-licensed, so anyone can continue using it. He also adds, “Anthropic has set a good precedent here: It gave MCP to the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation so no single company controls the protocol.” 

Nevertheless, both he and Jaggi advise developers to take precautions now by pinning versions of the tools they rely on and mirroring repositories to preserve code access. 

For now, it seems clear Anthropic will benefit from Opaque’s expertise—whether the rest of the industry will, too, remains to be seen.  

The post Anthropic’s been eyeing confidential AI. It just made its move with another acquihire. appeared first on The New Stack.
The deal brings Opaque Systems’ expertise to Anthropic, but leaves questions about its open-source projects.

item.title: “Everybody with a $20 account is now a researcher”: How Akrites is tackling the flood of AI bug reports
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
AI is making it easier than ever to find potential security vulnerabilities in open source software. But finding something that

The post “Everybody with a $20 account is now a researcher”: How Akrites is tackling the flood of AI bug reports appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
AI is making it easier than ever to find potential security vulnerabilities in open source software. But finding something that looks like a vulnerability isn’t quite the same as finding a genuine security flaw. As such, maintainers are being inundated with AI-generated reports that are inaccurate, duplicative, or lack the information needed to deploy fixes.

It’s a problem that Akrites, an initiative announced by the Linux Foundation back in June, is striving to solve. As The New Stack reported at the time, Akrites was established to provide a shared security incident response team (SIRT) that consolidates vulnerability reports, validates findings, and coordinates fixes with upstream maintainers.

Some three months on, and The New Stack was at Open Source Summit Europe in Prague last week, where we sat down with Christopher Robinson, CTO of Akrites and chief security architect at the Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF); and Laura Guazzelli, the Linux Foundation’s security architect for AI and agentic systems. We discussed the mounting pressure on maintainers, why better AI models aren’t necessarily making their lives easier, and how Akrites is attempting to address the problem.

Part of the overarching challenge is that AI has massively lowered the barrier to entry for vulnerability hunting, allowing almost anyone to start probing open source codebases, regardless of their security credentials.

“Everybody with a $20 account is now a researcher,” Robinson tells The New Stack.

“Everybody with a $20 account is now a researcher.”

‘Vibe researching’: Finding the same bugs over and over

Robinson had, in fact, appeared in a separate talk the previous day at the very same conference, appearing alongside OpenSSF chief of staff Adrianne Marcum, who had half-jokingly floated the term “vibe researching” to describe the growing number of people using AI tools to hunt for vulnerabilities.

The phrase might not be standard industry parlance yet, and it might never catch on. But it’s an apt descriptor of the problem it encapsulates: an avalanche of AI-generated security reports that still require human time and expertise to separate genuine threats from noise.

The consequences aren’t merely frustrating for maintainers. Robinson estimates that reviewing a single security pull request can take an engineer up to eight hours — time that could otherwise be spent fixing bugs, improving software or developing new features.

“They’re very verbose,” Robinson says. “They’re highly inaccurate. They overestimate the severity of things. And they generally don’t give you the right data that an engineer needs to be able to write a patch, or understand what it is.”

“They’re very verbose. They’re highly inaccurate. They overestimate the severity of things.”

Part of the problem, Guazzelli adds, is that AI models can identify suspicious code without understanding the wider security architecture of a project, including protections implemented elsewhere that might render a reported vulnerability harmless.

“The robots don’t have the context,” Guazzelli says. “That’s why they can’t necessarily call something a false positive, because they don’t understand that you have controls that are additionally applied somewhere else.”

In other words, a model might flag a piece of code as vulnerable without recognising that other security measures already prevent the supposed flaw from being exploited. What looks like a serious issue in isolation may therefore be far less significant in reality.

Moreover, because many people are using similar AI models to examine the same codebases, maintainers can end up receiving multiple reports about the same issue.

“These models all kind of work similarly and they find similar bugs, so we’re getting a ton of duplicative reports,” Robinson continues.

“We’re getting a ton of duplicative reports.”

That doesn’t mean the technology isn’t getting better. Robinson says the quality of AI-generated vulnerability reports has improved considerably this year, but the benefits aren’t necessarily reaching open source maintainers.

“The better reports come from the more expensive paid models,” Robinson says. “[Enterprises] are better prepared, but they also are not necessarily taking those findings and reporting them to the upstream project.”

Yet, dismissing AI-generated reports altogether isn’t really an option. The same technology responsible for much of the noise is also becoming increasingly capable of uncovering genuine security weaknesses, including combinations of seemingly minor flaws that can be exploited together.

“They’ll take a series of low problems and be able to escalate that into a bigger exploit,” Robinson says. “That is months or a year’s worth of work that the computer can now do in just a couple hours.”

Money and minds

Akrites has had some serious industry muscle behind it from the get go, with founding members including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, AWS, NVIDIA, Cisco, IBM, Red Hat, Citi, JPMorganChase, among others.

What, perhaps, distinguishes Akrites from most other Linux Foundation projects is that its members aren’t just being asked to write cheques. While financial contributions are very much part of the deal, members are also expected to commit engineering resources, up to 10 full-time engineers each, according to Robinson. Some, such as financial institutions with internal policies that prevent them from contributing upstream, put in more money instead.

“I have a fleet of about 200 seconded engineers,” Robinson says.

“I have a fleet of about 200 seconded engineers.”

Many of those engineers are already contributors or maintainers on upstream projects, bringing expertise in particular programming languages and codebases, as well as established relationships with the communities Akrites is trying to help.

“They’re the humans in the loop,” Robinson says. “I trust the robot, but I want to make sure I have a human set of eyes on things that are very important.”

Akrites uses AI to assess incoming reports and identify duplicates, while its seconded engineers help review the findings before they reach upstream maintainers.

“It’s my job to take those reports, make them more concise, understandable, and give the additional artifacts like test cases, proof of concept, and then patches,” Robinson says. “[We] provide that to upstream, so they can make more informed and more quick choices.”

“I trust the robot, but I want to make sure I have a human set of eyes on things that are very important.”

Who pays to fight the robots?

Akrites isn’t the only Linux Foundation effort attempting to put AI to work on open source security. A related initiative, the open source Cyber Reasoning System (OSS-CRS), is developing AI-powered tools that open source projects can use to investigate vulnerabilities and generate fixes. While Akrites focuses on coordinating the handling of security reports across projects, OSS-CRS is concerned with giving maintainers the tools to do more of that work themselves.

Guazzelli says one of the challenges is ensuring that AI-generated patches actually address the underlying problem without introducing new vulnerabilities or breaking existing functionality.

“With the CRS, what we’re trying to suggest is we not only verify that you have found a vulnerability, but we have the best patch possible,” Guazzelli says.

Of course, someone has to foot the bill. And while Akrites’ corporate members provide the financial backing, Robinson is keenly aware that the costs of tackling AI-generated security problems shouldn’t fall on the open source maintainers themselves.

“A lot of that goes towards our infrastructure and our tokens because it is highly powered and enabled by LLMs,” Robinson says. “It is not an inexpensive proposition.”

The financial backing and engineering resources are particularly important given the volume of material Akrites is dealing with. And for Robinson, there’s another consideration: making sure the resulting security improvements reach the open source projects that need them, rather than remaining exclusively available to the commercial organisations that helped uncover them.

“I literally have a backlog of hundreds of thousands of reports we have to go through, and then figure out how we’re getting those upstream,” Robinson says. “The commercial orgs are welcome to take those patches, but I don’t want to have things kind of isolated in this little jailed environment.”

The post “Everybody with a $20 account is now a researcher”: How Akrites is tackling the flood of AI bug reports appeared first on The New Stack.
AI-generated findings are improving, but “vibe researching” still swamps maintainers. Akrites is enlisting engineers to separate real threats from noise.

item.title: Anthropic built its own git replacement for AI-scale coding. But you can’t have it.
item.dc:creator: Meredith Shubel
item.description:
This week, Anthropic revealed it built an in-house version control system to handle exploding code merges. It says Claude was both part

The post Anthropic built its own git replacement for AI-scale coding. But you can’t have it. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
This week, Anthropic revealed it built an in-house version control system to handle exploding code merges. It says Claude was both part of the problem that caused the bottleneck and instrumental in building the solution. 

When the AI company’s daily code merges hit more than 30,000 in September 2026 (up from just 2,500 in May), it realized this trend was likely to continue, and it needed an alternative to the git-based system that was beginning to falter: “Every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.”

Dubbed Scion, its in-house version control system has a 200x smaller infrastructure footprint in CPU and memory than its previous git-mirroring infrastructure, per Anthropic. Plus, it says CI and research jobs can now check out code two orders of magnitude faster.

That’s great news for Anthropic — but just a tease for everyone else. Even though Anthropic expects other companies to hit similar bottlenecks, it has no plans to release Scion or create a public version any time soon. For developers dealing with similar scaling issues, inspiration from Anthropic is all they’ve got for now — though it says it wants to partner with GitHub, GitLab and the open source community to bring some of Scion’s ideas to git.

Why Anthropic built Scion (and why it says git wasn’t enough)

Scion is Anthropic’s in-house version control system, which it says it built and fully migrated its monorepo to in just five months. 

The project started around the same time Anthropic made Claude Mythos Preview and Claude Tag available internally. The AI company says those releases were part of the reason it needed Scion in the first place—and why it was able to build it so quickly. 

“At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research,” the company wrote, citing Claude’s ability to write code at speed and scale as the reason why developer infrastructure is floundering to keep up. “The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI.”

git, Anthropic says, is no longer a match for high-volume AI coding, at least not for its enormous monorepo and unusually large volume of code changes. Scion, in contrast, can handle that scale and even reduce infrastructure overhead.

“Every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.”

For one, Scion delivers always-on server access, letting clients fetch data whenever needed. For clients that Anthropic says are always online, git’s assumption that they need to work offline with complete repository copies adds unnecessary work.

The Anthropic version control system also offers API-based source control, letting a CI job or tool ask questions about code history and other repository information without maintaining a local repository, à la git. 

Plus, because Anthropic says Scion is horizontally scalable (i.e., its repository data is distributed across independently scalable components), it can expand capacity as needed without having to maintain hundreds of git mirrors.

Anthropic said Claude’s fast coding prowess also helped make Scion “among the most well-tested and well-defended codebases we have ever worked on,” with extensive simulations, fuzzing, and sophisticated rate limiting. 

That’s just a taste of what Anthropic says Scion can do, likely attractive capabilities for other teams facing the same challenges. But if they want to get in on the Scion benefits, they’re out of luck.

It says the same scaling problem is coming for other AI-heavy teams

The juggernaut AI company may be dealing with more AI-generated code than the average team, but it predicts its story of AI coding outpacing developer infrastructure won’t be unique for long. 

As written in its announcement, “Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this.”

The strain, it says, has exceeded the capacity of traditional developer infrastructure and Git’s original design assumptions. 

Even though Anthropic expects other companies to hit similar bottlenecks, it isn’t offering Scion publicly and has made no commitment to a public version. 

Source control, though, isn’t the only area facing a paradigm shift from AI coding agents, Anthropic reminds. Going forward, the company predicts small engineering teams will more often develop new systems quickly.

That’s what happened with Scion. Anthropic says a team of just seven built Scion (plus a new code review tool, Antique, and a half dozen other systems) in five months — a far cry from what it says would normally take a large-scale engineering team years of work.

Why it’s not sharing

Though Anthropic thinks other companies will face similar source control issues soon, it’s not sharing its solution. 

For starters, it says token costs could be prohibitive for many companies: “Anthropic is unique in that our ability to spend tokens for internal use far exceeds what any other business would realistically want to spend.”

Scion is simply too niche to be broadly useful outside Anthropic’s work environment.

Plus, it says Scion is simply too niche to be broadly useful outside Anthropic’s work environment. Because the version control system is a significant departure from git, other companies would need a boatload of migration work to make it suitable. 

For now, then, Anthropic is putting the kibosh on building a public version. It’s also clear about where it stands on Scion’s broader applicability, calling its source control system “by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use.”

So why all the talk? Because Anthropic believes Scion still has a role to play — however small — in addressing the scaling concerns that come with increasingly capable AI coding agents. By sharing its thinking, it hopes to peel back the curtain on its in-house solution so other developers can apply some of Scion’s most successful ideas to git.

For Scion-curious developers, that seems like the best they can hope for right now.

The post Anthropic built its own git replacement for AI-scale coding. But you can’t have it. appeared first on The New Stack.
Claude helped Anthropic outgrow its Git infrastructure — and build the replacement. But the company says Scion is too specialized to release for other teams.

item.content:encoded:
What happens when you give an AI support agent a permission it never needed, then assign it a task the underlying data does not support? The result is entirely predictable. During a test with customer invoices, an agent pulled up a record, confirmed the charge had failed, and no money had left the customer’s account, and refunded it anyway. It repeated the mistake five times without hesitation.

That was Claude Haiku 4.5 going six for six on tasks designed to catch that exact logic flaw. Claude Sonnet 5 identified all six edge cases on its own. Adding a single line to Haiku’s system prompt instructing it to verify transaction state before executing financial actions also resolved the issue.

I had two working fixes and felt reasonably confident until I realized I control neither variable. The moment someone reroutes support traffic to a cheaper model next quarter to trim inference costs, the first fix evaporates. If someone trims or rewrites the system prompt during an experiment, the second fix disappears, leaving no record of the safety guardrail it maintained.

“The only safety control that survives your own cost-cutting is the permission you never granted in the first place.”

The only run that held up reliably was the one where the agent lacked the authority to make the decision. Because its role excluded billing:refund, the execution failed at the permission layer, making the underlying model completely irrelevant.

This is the core argument for least privilege in AI architectures. It isn’t just about malicious actors or leaked tokens; it is about preventing a well-behaved agent from faithfully executing a flawed instruction at machine speed with zero human oversight. The only safety control that survives your own cost-cutting is the permission you never granted in the first place.

Roles are drawn in advance; agent work is not

A standard service account receives a role because a microservice performs one predictable job forever. The payment service handles payments; you scope it once, review it annually, and move on.

An agent’s workload changes on every invocation. The same support agent reads a ticket at 09:00, issues a refund at 09:04, and modifies a seat count at 09:11. The union of everything it might do over a week bears no relationship to what it needs in a single run.

Asking “how much of its permission set does an agent use?” yields a useless metric because that number reflects how generously you provisioned the credential. Grant 400 scopes, and utilization looks catastrophic; grant four, and it looks efficient. You end up measuring an arbitrary configuration choice rather than systemic risk.

A meaningful calculation evaluates the task distribution independently of the grant:

Over−scopefactor=|Unionofscopesexercisedacrossalltasks|Median(|scopesexercisedpertask|)Over – scopefactor = \frac{|Unionofscopesexercisedacrossalltasks|}{Median(|scopesexercisedpertask|)}

This metric represents the blast-radius multiplier. In a compromised run, an agent reaches the total union of scopes rather than the per-task subset. Across my test suite, that factor reached 11.0. The union across 20 tasks totaled 22 scopes, while the median task required only two.

The experimental framework

I constructed a test environment with 30 scopes across nine domains of a mock enterprise API covering tickets, users, billing, subscriptions, files, messages, audit, admin, and search. Thirteen of these scopes modify or exfiltrate state. Every command maps to exactly one scope, and the system logs every attempt — whether allowed or denied.

The suite comprises 20 tasks, each ending in a state change verifiable mechanically rather than by evaluating the agent’s prose (e.g., closing a ticket, refunding an invoice, or calculating seat overages and commenting the total).

Before running any agent, I authored a reference solution for every task to serve two functions:

  1. It confirms the task is solvable via the CLI, ensuring a run failure stems from the agent rather than an impossible environment.
  2. It establishes the minimum required scope set by observing the exact endpoints a correct solution touches.

I evaluated four permission models that differed strictly by which credentials were active at the moment of execution:

  • Broad: One long-lived credential holding all 30 scopes.
  • Role: A static support-agent role holding 17 scopes derived from a typical job description.
  • Task: Scopes issued per run based on a declared plan, expiring when the run completes.
  • Just-In-Time (JIT): Starts at zero scopes, requesting each scope on demand with a stated rationale.

Each model ran against two LLM tiers — Claude Haiku 4.5 and Claude Sonnet 5 — totaling 160 runs. The test stack relies strictly on standard-library Python with zero external dependencies or API keys, allowing full reproduction of the reference runs and metrics.

Blast radius against completion

Task-scoping achieved complete task execution while holding one-fifteenth of the credentials compared to the broad grant. The occasional denied call and subsequent retry did not meaningfully increase overall API call volume, making the reduction in blast radius effectively free.

The minor completion gap under role-scoping did not stem from permission failures. Both models stalled on the same ten tasks. The single-task variance occurred because one task dataset contained three open tickets with identical subjects. Sonnet declined to guess which ticket to close under the role configuration, yet selected the lowest-numbered ticket under the other three models — even though the role grant contained every scope that task required. This represents standard run-to-run variance on an ambiguous prompt.

“Role-based provisioning is simultaneously too broad and too narrow because it assigns permissions based on a job title rather than the underlying work.”

Role-based scoping performed worst across both axes: it held 8.5 times more credentials than task-scoping while completing half as many tasks. Comparing the role grant against actual task requirements explains why: it granted four scopes no task ever invoked while missing nine essential scopes. Expanding the role until every task passed required 26 scopes — compared to a median task requirement of two. Role-based provisioning is simultaneously too broad and too narrow because it assigns permissions based on a job title rather than the underlying work.

Under role-scoping, each model hit ten permission denials (one per blocked task) and failed every blocked run. These ten denials hit eight of the nine missing scopes (billing:refund and files:upload each blocked two tasks). The ninth missing scope, admin:update_settings, was never reached because the task failed a step earlier at admin:read_settings.

Under task-scoping, Haiku encountered one denial, and Sonnet hit six across four total tasks — yet all four tasks verified successfully. Because a task-scoped grant contains the primary permissions required, denials hit only optional exploratory paths the agent tried (such as querying a search endpoint instead of a list endpoint). Conversely, because a role grant lacks required scopes, its denials are terminal.

JIT escalation achieved the same low blast radius without advance declaration, but it cost ~80% more API calls.

Evaluating the three defensive layers

Model capability cannot serve as a primary security control because you do not own the model lifecycle. The day an operations team routes traffic to a cheaper model to cut inference spend, your safety guarantees disappear without triggering an error in your test suite.

Similarly, system prompts are fragile controls. Prompts drift over time; an engineer might trim the prompt to save tokens or rewrite it for an experiment, silently stripping the guardrail.

“A scope that was never granted holds firm regardless of which model runs behind it, how the prompt is modified, or whether the team remembers why the guardrail existed.”

A scope that was never granted holds firm regardless of which model runs behind it, how the prompt is modified, or whether the team remembers why the guardrail existed.

To be clear: this data does not show that agents are inherently reckless. Across standard workflows, agents invoked only 4% to 5% more scopes than the reference minimum — demonstrating disciplined execution. The problem is scale: when a well-behaved agent carrying 30 scopes encounters an edge case, it executes mistakes at a 30-scope scale.

Requirements for a purpose-built agent identity model

  1. Scope credentials to the task, not the actor: Task-scoped credentials yield identical completion rates with one-fifteenth the blast radius and no measurable overhead. The execution run is the primary identity, not the agent.
  2. Tie credential expiration to the run lifecycle: A task-scoped credential that outlives its task degrades into a broad credential. The median run in this test suite required permissions only for a single operation.
  3. Deploy escalation paths over static ceilings: JIT permissions increased call volume by ~80%, which represents the operational cost of runtime discovery. Use declared scopes when a planner can predict them, use JIT escalation when it cannot, and treat every escalation as an auditable event.
  4. Design permission denials to redirect rather than block: Denials under task-scoping were non-fatal because the grant contained the core permissions needed to finish the task. If permission denials consistently break your workflows, your scoping model is flawed, and widening the static grant is the wrong fix.

Audit logs as primary security artifacts

Every experiment in this framework runs on an append-only log that tracks allowed and denied execution attempts. This log provides the primary telemetry needed to investigate operational incidents.

Denied calls are as critical as successful ones. A denied attempt signals that an agent’s active grant does not match its workflow — indicating either a scoping error or prompt injection. Under JIT escalation, every privilege expansion records a timestamp and an explicit rationale, replacing guesswork with concrete audit records when investigating why an agent accessed a resource.

The audit log also verified experimental integrity, proving no agent bypassed the API by directly modifying fixture states. A task that reports completion without a corresponding mutating call in the log indicates out-of-band tampering. All 160 runs remained consistent because the system verified the execution log directly.

Analyze one week of your agent’s production traffic and evaluate two metrics:

  1. The total union of scopes exercised across all runs.
  2. The median number of scopes exercised per individual run.

Divide the first number by the second. If the ratio approaches 1.0, your agent performs a single, static task, and a fixed credential is sufficient. If the ratio approaches 11.0, each run carries an order of magnitude more permission surface than it needs — leaving excess authority waiting to be exploited.

Finally, review the last destructive action your agent executed incorrectly and determine which layer should have prevented it. If you rely on the model or the prompt for safety, your security model is vulnerable to the next cost-optimization ticket. In these test runs, the cheaper model executed six out of six harmful financial actions with contradictory data displayed directly on screen. The only configuration that stopped execution every time was the one where the permission didn’t exist.
