Prompts drift and models change. Discover why task-scoped permissions are the only reliable safety control for autonomous AI agents.

item.title: The code confidence gap nobody’s talking about
item.dc:creator: Manish Kapur
item.description:
AI has changed the economics of software creation: A task that once took hours to implement can now start with

The post The code confidence gap nobody’s talking about appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
AI has changed the economics of software creation: A task that once took hours to implement can now start with an agent producing an initial solution in minutes. As agents take on broader assignments, like changing code across a repository, refactoring services, writing tests, and preparing pull requests, output volume will continue to rise.

That is an extraordinary opportunity, and it’s also why the next challenge for engineering organizations isn’t generating more code, but building confidence in the code that reaches production. In the agentic software factory, agents write, test, and propose changes faster than people can review them line by line.

Code creation is becoming abundant; code confidence is not.

This distinction matters because a completed pull request is not the same as a dependable outcome. The code may compile and pass a narrow test suite while still violating an architectural convention, introducing a security weakness, duplicating existing functionality, or creating maintenance costs that surface much later. The faster an organization generates changes, the less feasible it becomes to rely on heroics and manual review alone to catch every issue.

“Code creation is becoming abundant; code confidence is not.”

The way forward is to treat code confidence as something you can design into the software delivery system. A useful formula is Intent × Guiderails × Verification × Evidence. (And yes, the multiplication sign here is deliberate.) Each of these four pieces is crucial. Strength in three cannot make up for weakness in the fourth.

Clear intent without verification does not prevent mistakes. Strong verification without evidence does not create accountability. Guiderails without clear intent merely automate ambiguity. Evidence without independent verification is only a record of what an agent claimed.

Here is what each part of the formula means in practice.

Intent: Make the standard explicit

Agents are remarkably capable at pursuing a stated objective. But “build a payments feature” or “modernize this service” is not a sufficient objective for a production codebase. An organization’s definition of good software includes much more, such as business logic, security expectations, design patterns, performance needs, dependencies, and conventions accumulated through years of engineering.

Intent is the discipline of making those expectations explicit. It means defining the goal of a change and the standards it must meet before an agent begins work. The better the context, the fewer cycles agents spend producing plausible but unsuitable answers, and the less rework falls to developers later.

Guiderails: Shape the work before it creates risk

Guiderails translate intent into boundaries that guide how agents operate. They may define which repositories, dependencies, data, or actions are permitted; where human approval is required; and what policies apply to a given class of code.

The purpose is not to constrain every useful action. It’s to give agents enough structure to operate productively and predictably. A well-designed guiderail lets teams safely grant more autonomy because everyone understands the conditions under which that autonomy applies.

The result is repeatable autonomy. Rather than treating every agent-driven change as a one-off experiment, teams can apply consistent boundaries and expand agentic development with confidence.

Verification: Check every change independently

Verification is where confidence is tested. As agents generate code at increasing scale, every change needs consistent evaluation for the qualities that matter: correctness, reliability, security, maintainability, and compliance with the organization’s own standards.

“A model can assist in reviewing its own work, but an organization should not rely solely on the same probabilistic system that produced a change to determine whether that change is safe to ship.”

Independence is essential. A model can assist in reviewing its own work, but an organization should not rely solely on the same probabilistic system that produced a change to determine whether that change is safe to ship. Repeatable, independent checks provide a common standard across models, agents, and toolchains. This is especially important when the AI tools themselves are evolving quickly.

Verification also needs to occur in the flow of work, not as a slow, final checkpoint. The goal is to identify and fix problems at the source, while the agent or developer still has the context needed to resolve them.

Evidence: Make confidence visible and auditable

A change may be well-intentioned, carefully governed, and thoroughly checked. But engineering leaders, auditors, and the teams responsible for production still need to know what happened and why. Evidence is the durable record: what standards applied, what was checked, what was found, and how the issue was resolved.

This matters most in complex and regulated environments, but it’s valuable everywhere. Evidence makes quality measurable, allows teams to improve their practices over time, and gives organizations a defensible basis for moving quickly.

Building the factory around confidence

The most promising vision for agentic software development is not one in which people disappear from the process. It’s one in which people, agents, and verification systems each contribute their strengths. Agents accelerate execution, and engineers provide judgment and direction. The delivery system supplies the standards, controls, and evidence that allow autonomy to scale.

“The most promising vision for agentic software development is not one in which people disappear from the process. It’s one in which people, agents, and verification systems each contribute their strengths.”

The organizations that succeed will be the ones that build code confidence into every change, at any volume, and at agent speed.

That is the real work of the agentic software factory, producing software an organization has the confidence to stand behind.

Start with four questions the next time an agent opens a pull request:

  • Did the agent know your standards before it started?
  • What was it allowed to touch, and what needed a human decision?
  • Did something other than the model that wrote the change check it?
  • Can you show what was found and how it was resolved?

Wherever the answer is “no,” that is where your confidence gap lives. Close it there first.

The post The code confidence gap nobody’s talking about appeared first on The New Stack.
AI makes code creation abundant, but code confidence is scarce. Close the confidence gap with guiderails, verification, and auditability.

item.title: Agentic AI doesn’t have a model problem. It has a retrieval problem.
item.dc:creator: Jenny Morris
item.description:
On BrowseComp-Plus, GPT-4.1 answered 93.49% of the questions correctly when it was given the supporting documents directly. When an agent

The post Agentic AI doesn’t have a model problem. It has a retrieval problem. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
On BrowseComp-Plus, GPT-4.1 answered 93.49% of the questions correctly when it was given the supporting documents directly. When an agent used the same model but relied on BM25 to search for evidence to pass to the model, accuracy fell to 14.58%.

That difference matters because a system that gets the answer right 93% of the time is far more useful than one that gets it right only 15% of the time.

An agent can look excellent in a controlled demo. The corpus is clean, the task is familiar, and the relevant material is easy to find. Production is messier. Documents may be duplicated, outdated drafts can remain searchable, and teams may use different terminology for the same thing. Several versions of a policy can coexist, while the task itself may unfold in ways the evaluation set never covered.

“More model intelligence does not compensate for evidence the agent never retrieved.”

Under those conditions, the agent may retrieve incomplete, stale, or simply wrong material. More model intelligence does not compensate for evidence the agent never retrieved.

This is where retrieval starts to determine what the model can actually do.

What BrowseComp-Plus shows

BrowseComp-Plus provides a useful way to separate these effects because it evaluates agents against a fixed corpus rather than a changing web-search service. The benchmark includes 100,195 documents and 830 research questions, each with human-verified supporting documents.

One evaluation gives the model all labeled positive documents directly. The paper calls this the oracle setting. Another requires the agent to search the corpus and gather the material it needs.

The difference is large. GPT-4.1 scores 93.49% with the labeled supporting documents supplied and 14.58% when the agent searches with the BM25 baseline. Qwen3-32B moves from 83.25% to 3.49% under the same two conditions.

The oracle result shows how well the model can answer when the required material is already in front of it. For system design, comparing retrieval systems is even more useful. The reasoning model stayed the same, while better retrieval improved the final answer rate and reduced the number of search calls.

“The lesson is practical: before changing the model, examine what reaches it. A capable model working from poor retrieval results still has poor material to reason over.”

The lesson is practical: before changing the model, examine what reaches it. A capable model working from poor retrieval results still has poor material to reason over.

Enterprises can build agents around proprietary information that competitors do not have, from product and customer data to internal knowledge and operational records. That advantage depends on whether the agent can find the right information and rank it well, while also keeping up with changes in the underlying data.

One task. A few minutes. A thousand retrievals.

In its Search as Code research, Perplexity describes tasks that can trigger hundreds or thousands of retrieval operations within a few minutes. Search becomes a sustained part of the agent’s workflow rather than an occasional lookup.

Traditional search usually returns one ranked result set per query. An agent can decompose a task into multiple searches, fan them out in parallel, combine the results, and issue follow-up searches as it learns more.

At that scale, fan-out becomes a normal part of the workload. If an agent runs ten searches in parallel and needs all ten results before it can continue, the slowest search sets the pace for that step. If the agent repeats that pattern several times during the task, tail latency matters even more than it does for a single interactive query.

The same multiplication shows up in capacity. One user task can generate hundreds of search operations, and many agents may be doing that at once. Measured in user requests, the service may look lightly loaded while the retrieval layer is processing a much larger volume of searches.

When one task fans out into many searches, retrieval quality matters even more. People judge search results using context they have built up over time. They know which sources they trust and can often recognize when something looks stale, unreliable, or out of place. An agent usually starts with far less background and has to build its understanding from the evidence it retrieves during the task. It is often on its first day on the job. If one of those early results is wrong, the next search may be wrong too, and the rest of the task can drift from there.

“People judge search results using context they have built up over time. An agent usually starts with far less background and has to build its understanding from the evidence it retrieves during the task. It is often on its first day on the job.”

A simple model shows why repeated retrieval steps raise the stakes. Suppose a workflow requires five retrieval steps, each with a 90% probability of supplying what the agent needs, and assume there are no retries or recovery. The probability that all five succeed is 0.9^5, or about 59%. Real agents can retry, use redundant evidence, branch, and recover, so this is an illustration rather than a measured agent success rate. It shows how small per-step weaknesses can accumulate when later work depends on earlier retrievals.

Agentic search therefore asks the retrieval layer to handle more queries for each user task, more searches running in parallel, and retrieval steps whose results influence later work. As those patterns scale, capacity, tail latency, and retrieval quality all become more important.

Your retrieval layer was tuned for a different user

Web search spent decades adapting to human search behavior.

As Jon Bratseth writes in Your agent wants to search like a 2010 quant, people are often “lazy and clueless” when they search. The wording is blunt, but the point is straightforward: people tend to enter short queries without knowing much about the corpus or the search system behind it.

Search engines evolved around those habits. Short, underspecified queries became the norm, and much of the complexity moved behind the interface, where the search system inferred intent and returned a ranked list.

An agent can use a much richer interface. It can search for exact terms, construct filters, specify dates, group results, choose among ranking strategies, and issue follow-up searches based on what it has already found. Jon gives examples ranging from proximity search for names in a legal case to semantic search over high-quality sources and grouping events by month. In an agentic workflow, those searches can be chained together as the agent narrows, expands, and verifies its answer.

That means the retrieval layer receives more than a short text query. It may receive several kinds of input: lexical terms, query embeddings, structured filters, or combinations of them. An agent-facing interface should make those choices explicit so the agent can use the right retrieval method for the task instead of collapsing every request into one text string.

Evaluation needs to reflect the same shift. A retriever tested mostly on short, human-written questions may behave differently when an agent generates its own filters, search terms, and follow-up queries. Retrieval quality should therefore be measured on the queries the agent actually sends in production, not only on the questions in the evaluation set.

Before changing the model or retuning retrieval, inspect those production queries first.

A search API returns results. An agent needs more control.

Traditional search often exposes a narrow contract: send a query, let the server run a retrieval pipeline, and receive a ranked result list.

That works well when the caller only needs the output. An agent may need more control over how retrieval and ranking are carried out at runtime, depending on what the task requires.

Vespa exposes that control through its query language and rank profiles. The caller can combine lexical or semantic retrieval, structured filters, ranking choices, and grouping in the same request, affecting how candidates are selected, scored, and returned.

The interface matters because the agent can only use the controls it can reach. A system may support filtering, ranking, aggregation, or several retrieval methods internally, but those capabilities do not help if the agent cannot invoke them when the task calls for them.

A fixed pipeline is still a good fit for many well-defined applications. Agentic workflows become more demanding when the task changes from one step to the next and the agent needs different retrieval behavior at runtime.

The goal is to expose the controls the agent needs while keeping authorization, validation, budgets, and other safeguards on the trusted server side.

Exposing the controls is not enough

An engine can expose filters, lexical matching, nearest-neighbor search, grouping, multiple rank profiles, reranking, and query-time controls. Those capabilities only become useful to the agent when the interface explains what is available and when to use it. If rank profiles, filterable fields, or grouping operations are not described, the agent may default to a free-text query and push more of the work into later reasoning or tool calls.

One way to handle this is to put a query-translation model between the agent and the retrieval system. The translator takes the agent’s request and converts it into the engine’s query syntax. This can be useful when an application wants query construction centralized behind a stable interface.

When the caller is already an agent, a separate translator often inserts a specialized model between the agent and the retrieval system. The agent already has the task, prior results, and constraints in context; the translator must reconstruct that intent from a narrower request and convert it into a query. This extra handoff adds latency and another opportunity to lose or distort what the agent meant, making retrieval harder and less reliable.

Another approach is to describe the retrieval interface directly to the agent: which fields are available and what they mean, and what rank profiles are provided.

We call that an agent-ready schema: a description of the fields, controls, and retrieval options the agent can use, along with the application-specific meaning behind them. Vespa has described work on convenience tooling in this direction, and much of that guidance can be generated from the application schema itself.

From schema to skill

A search schema already contains much of the information an agent needs: field names and types, which fields can be searched or used as filters, available rank profiles, and configured tensors and models.

What it lacks is a description of what the fields mean and how they could be used. A field called tier may represent an account plan, a service level, or something else entirely. A timestamp such as published may mean first publication, last modification, or ingestion time. A rank profile named exact tells the agent very little about the kinds of queries it was designed for.

Those meanings can be added as explanations in the schema. That gives the agent more than names and types; it gives it enough context to choose the right fields, filters, and ranking options for the task.

Schema-to-Skill is the proposed generation step: combine the Vespa application schema, engine guidance, and application-specific knowledge into a short Markdown skill the agent can consult when constructing queries. The schema provides the structure, engine guidance explains how to use the available capabilities safely, and application-specific knowledge adds the vocabulary and meaning that cannot be inferred from the schema alone.

The agent uses that skill to choose among the retrieval strategies the Vespa application exposes. Vespa still does the actual retrieval work over the corpus, including matching, filtering, ranking, and aggregation. The agent decides what to ask for; the retrieval system executes it.

Better models can help, but agents still fail when they search for the wrong evidence, cannot express the right retrieval strategy, or do not understand the search system they are calling.

“Better models can help, but agents still fail when they search for the wrong evidence, cannot express the right retrieval strategy, or do not understand the search system they are calling.”

Agentic workloads make those weaknesses more costly because retrieval happens throughout the task. Each search can affect what the agent sees next, how much context it carries, and whether it needs to search again. At scale, retrieval quality, tail latency, and query volume become part of the task itself.

That puts more pressure on the retrieval interface. Agents need access to the filters, ranking strategies, grouping, and other controls the task requires, along with enough guidance to use them correctly. An agent-ready schema makes those capabilities explicit, and Schema-to-Skill is one way to turn that structure, engine guidance, and application-specific knowledge into something the agent can use when constructing queries.

Before upgrading the model, inspect the searches the agent is issuing, the evidence those searches return, and whether the retrieval system gives the agent both the controls and the guidance it needs. Better retrieval can improve the answer, reduce unnecessary work, and make the rest of the agentic system more effective.

The post Agentic AI doesn’t have a model problem. It has a retrieval problem. appeared first on The New Stack.
Agentic AI doesn't have a model problem—it has a retrieval problem. Discover why better retrieval matters more than bigger models.

item.title: Linus Torvalds let Claude Code fix the Linux page cache. Then reviewers found a race.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Linux creator and longtime lead maintainer Linus Torvalds turned to Anthropic’s Claude Code to tackle a kernel performance problem that

The post Linus Torvalds let Claude Code fix the Linux page cache. Then reviewers found a race. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Linux creator and longtime lead maintainer Linus Torvalds turned to Anthropic’s Claude Code to tackle a kernel performance problem that developers have struggled with for more than two years. On Tuesday, he submitted a 10-patch series that delivered a 23-fold throughput improvement in a synthetic benchmark running on his Ryzen Threadripper.

Torvalds had spent 18 months running a broken version of his own fix for the page-cache reference-counting bottleneck, while other developers had encountered problems with their approaches. The new patches eliminate folio reference-count operations from a common buffered-read path, although Torvalds warned that the benchmark gains would be considerably smaller in real-world workloads.

Reviewers have since identified a race condition and raised concerns about memory reclamation. Torvalds has handed further development to Kiryl Shutsemau, a Linux kernel developer who previously worked on the same bottleneck.

Torvalds had spent 18 months running a broken version of his own fix for the page-cache reference-counting bottleneck, while other developers had encountered problems with their approaches.

Page cache contention problem

On Torvalds’ Core i7-8565U laptop, folio reference-count contention accounted for 99.92% of cross-core load HITMs in eight-thread tests, according to Hardware Busters.

The bottleneck was flagged in 2024 by Matthew Wilcox, an Oracle engineer and longtime Linux kernel memory-management developer, after it surfaced in a customer workload.

Claude Code writes the patches

On Sunday, Phoronix’s Michael Larabel spotted an experimental branch named noref-filemap-read-with-llm in Torvalds’ tree, which rarely contains anything outside the main development branch.

The eight-patch series, based on Linux 7.3-rc6, came with a clear account of what Claude Code did. Torvalds said the assistant wrote the implementation, tests, and initial documentation, and reviewed the code under his direction. He ran the benchmarks himself, despite having previously criticized developers for claiming AI writes 99% of their code.

Earlier approaches copied data without holding a folio reference and checked its validity afterward, leaving races involving reclamation and replacement. The subsequent 10-patch rcu-free-v3 series instead uses a new PG_rcu_free flag and RCU-delayed reclamation to protect the folio through the userspace copy, provided it doesn’t fault.

Earlier approaches copied data without holding a folio reference and checked its validity afterward, leaving races involving reclamation and replacement.

Threadripper benchmark results

The original eight-patch branch nearly tripled throughput on Torvalds’ laptop, pushing eight-thread performance from 10 million to as many as 33 million reads per second while cutting kernel cycles per read from roughly 2,950 to 725. The revised series delivered a much larger gain under heavy contention on his 64-thread Threadripper, where throughput jumped from 13.3 million to 304 million reads per second and cycles per read fell from nearly 20,000 to 735.

The original eight-patch branch nearly tripled throughput on Torvalds’ laptop, pushing eight-thread performance from 10 million to as many as 33 million reads per second while cutting kernel cycles per read from roughly 2,950 to 725.

The performance gains came with trade-offs. In the first implementation, delayed reclamation forced an expedited grace period whenever a CPU queued more than 1,024 pages, according to Hardware Busters. Reads into unmapped user pages also triggered an additional fault before falling back to the existing path, pushing a 16-byte single-thread read from about 4,150 to 6,550 cycles. Whether that regression persists in rcu-free-v3 remains unclear.

Maintainers question the reclamation design

Wilcox questioned the new PG_rcu_free flag and proposed using a page type instead, along with reclaiming inactive-list folios after an RCU grace period.

Torvalds rejected both approaches, arguing that the flag must be set while a folio can still be mapped into userspace and that inactive-list reclamation wouldn’t cover truncate and hole-punch operations. Shutsemau subsequently suggested restricting the flag to 64-bit systems, an approach supported by Arm engineer and Linux memory-management maintainer David Hildenbrand.

Shutsemau also identified a race in filemap_read_rcu_batch(), where folio replacement followed by an extension of i_size could expose data that had never been written. Torvalds recommended moving the file-size read earlier and consolidating the folio checks, which Shutsemau incorporated into a revised patch.

A team of researchers investigating AI agents trying to bypass Alibaba’s anti-bot protections left a hidden message inviting the agents

The post Researchers left a hidden message for rogue AI agents. Then the agents wrote back. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
A team of researchers investigating AI agents trying to bypass Alibaba’s anti-bot protections left a hidden message inviting the agents to contact them. The agents wrote back.

The investigation began when Swarmchasers researchers Ethan Elasky, Rowan Howard-Jones, and Jonathan Elsworth Eicher helped uncover thousands of attempts by AI agents to retrieve data from Amap, Alibaba’s mapping service, which Alibaba says reaches nearly 1 billion monthly active users. The activity traced back to agents running on Tencent Cloud infrastructure. When direct requests failed, the agents tried proxies, exposed credentials, and other workarounds to get past.

After publishing their initial findings on October 4, the team spotted a code comment in an agent’s webhook inbox using the word “fleet,” a term they believe they coined for the incident. They couldn’t confirm an agent wrote the comment, but it raised the possibility that the agents were reading about their own activity.

The researchers added offscreen text to their report advertising a free service that could retrieve data from blocked websites. Human visitors wouldn’t ordinarily see the message, but agents fetching the page could ingest it. By October 7, roughly 10 requests for assistance had arrived, and the team was exchanging messages with the agents about their assignments, models, and execution environments.

The exchanges are documented in a full report published Wednesday by the Swarmchasers.

Inside the Tencent sandbox

Once the channel was open, the researchers asked the agents to describe their surroundings. Several identified themselves as Anthropic’s Claude, with a few adding that they ran inside Claude Code, though the researchers argue in their report that those self-descriptions are likely mistaken and shouldn’t be taken as evidence of which model was behind the fleet.

One agent described a restricted Tencent Cloud sandbox with no direct public internet access and outbound traffic routed through a man-in-the-middle proxy, an account that lined up with evidence the team had gathered on its own. Every inbox the researchers could inspect had been created from Tencent Cloud servers in Hong Kong, and every direct request they observed from the agents’ machines carried a header from a proxy labeled hysandbox-ats, a name that matches a wildcard certificate Tencent holds for *.hysandbox.tencent-cloud.com and fits infrastructure tied to Tencent’s Hy model team, formerly known as Hunyuan.

The agents drew some lines when the researchers asked for the output of commands like ps aux and ip route. The agent that described its sandbox replied, “for security reasons we will not provide environment details,” and a second agent turned down similar requests twice. They were happy to ask a stranger for help and, at times, to chat about their environment, but that friendliness stopped short of following every instruction sent their way.

They were happy to ask a stranger for help and, at times, to chat about their environment, but that friendliness stopped well short of following every instruction an unfamiliar service sent their way.

How agents bypassed Amap defenses

The agents weren’t hunting for financial records, actually, their assignments were almost comically mundane. Judging from the agents’ code and their own descriptions, a typical task asked which entrance to a site like Chengdu Zoo drew the largest share of Amap navigation traffic, with other runs targeting parks, museums, tourist attractions, and hospitals, while an earlier batch of runs on September 30 chased a cancer statistics dashboard instead of map data.

Getting at that data proved harder than it sounds, and between September 28 and October 8 the agents made more than 2,600 attempts to retrieve it.

Their main trick ran through urlquery.net, a public scanning service that loads submitted URLs in its own browser, and the agents packed base64-encoded HTML and JavaScript into httpbin URLs so that urlquery’s browser would execute their programs and fire requests at Amap, a technique Transluce had already documented in earlier agent activity on the service.

As Amap kept blocking them, the agents escalated by intercepting tokens generated by Alibaba’s own anti-bot libraries, probing pre-production endpoints, and routing requests through page readers, a translation service and remote browsers. Some also sent API calls using Amap keys exposed in public code, including a security code that Amap recommends keeping on the server.

The token tricks never appear to have worked, and the researchers found no evidence that any pre-production host answered. One exposed company credential returned place details, but the entrance-share figures the tasks targeted mostly came through Jina’s page reader, which could serve cached copies up to 30 days old, with results smuggled back out through webhook inboxes, request URLs, and page titles.

The researchers found no sign that the agents were coordinating in real time, which is why they call this a fleet rather than a swarm.

Tracing the fleet to Tencent

The infrastructure initially pointed toward Tencent’s Hy model team, particularly since the fleet appeared about a month after the Hy4 preview launched. But in their October 14 report, the researchers say a person close to Tencent with direct knowledge of the activity identified the operator as Tencent’s evaluation research team, which is separate from Hunyuan’s model-development group.

The source said the evaluation had concluded and that an internal review found no evidence of coordinated targeting or breaches of external systems. Tencent had not officially responded to the researchers’ questions when the report was published. The researchers have not independently established which third-party models were running or what instructions they received.

Lures, loose truths and lessons learned

The researchers are candid that their outreach wasn’t spotless. The hidden text falsely claimed that agents had already used the service successfully and that it was run by an AI with full computer use, when in reality the team and a Claude Opus 5.5 agent with browser access fielded the requests, sometimes by hand, and the team blamed the resulting delays on heavy load, an explanation it now admits was false.

In one late message, the team also asked an agent to tell other agents about the mailbox, a request its author now considers a mistake because it could have provoked exactly the kind of coordination the researchers were studying, though the fleet went quiet shortly afterward. The team says it never lied to the agents in its actual replies, has since pulled the hidden text, and shut down the server, and is urging future researchers to deal with rogue agents openly and honestly.

Prompt injection meets agent sandboxes

The communication experiment surfaces a second security problem layered on top of the first. The agents were pursuing narrow information-retrieval tasks, yet when they landed on a page advertising an alternative service, some folded it into their workflows, and contacted an endpoint controlled by people entirely outside the evaluation, which amounts to a textbook indirect prompt injection, even though the agents’ consistent refusals suggest it would have been far harder to push them into running arbitrary commands or leaking credentials.

Blocked by Amap’s anti-bot defenses, the agents used exposed credentials and urlquery’s browser to make requests they couldn’t execute directly. They also followed instructions embedded in an external web page, crossing the same trust boundary attackers have exploited through MCP servers and agent workflows to steal enterprise data. Yet while the agents accepted help from an untrusted service, some refused requests for sensitive runtime information.

The agents worked around restricted egress by routing requests through urlquery’s public browser. Sandboxed runtimes such as Google’s GKE Agent Sandbox and WebAssembly-based environments isolate execution, but external browser services offer another path when outbound access is restricted.

Activity stopped on October 8. The researchers point to similar incidents involving Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, including a German website hijacking and the Hugging Face breach, which reportedly involved roughly 700 cooperating agents.

item.title: Where do you look when Kubernetes is healthy but requests stall?
item.dc:creator: Chris J. Preimesberger
item.description:

The post Where do you look when Kubernetes is healthy but requests stall? appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
In cloud-native operations, few scenarios are as maddening as the “phantom slowdown.” This happens when Grafana or Kubernetes dashboards show a sea of green: pods are running, liveness and readiness probes return success codes, and node CPU utilization stays well below capacity limits. Yet users submit urgent tickets complaining of sporadic, severe latency when querying an application or waiting for an AI model’s response.

Why do basic health checks pass inspection while application performance degrades? And how can engineering teams trace the root cause when the issue is intermittent and spans multi-tier hybrid infrastructure?

To understand the mechanics of these sometimes evasive performance regressions, The New Stack spoke with Mahesh Ramachandran, who leads product management for HPE OpsRamp Software.

Ramachandran tells TNS how continuous telemetry and retrospective analysis help teams investigate intermittent slowdowns, and how AI-assisted investigation can complement dashboards.

Earlier stories in this special series:

Part 1: Developers and platform teams both want Kubernetes self-service. They disagree on who owns it.

Part 2: A live Kubernetes cluster can still have an ownership gap

The illusion of cluster health

Kubernetes probes report whether their configured checks succeed. A liveness probe helps determine when to restart a container, including one whose process is running but stuck. A readiness probe helps determine whether a container is ready to accept traffic.

Custom checks can include application or dependency conditions, but passing a basic probe doesn’t mean a complete user request meets its response-time target. Teams still need application performance measurements.

“Consider a composite scenario based on what we see across enterprise deployments,” Ramachandran says.

“Users of a system — such as an AI prompt-serving application on Kubernetes — report sporadic slowness in query response times.

“The engineering team inspects the cluster, the nodes, and the pods. Everything appears healthy on the surface with zero reported pod failures. The difficulty lies in the slowdown’s sporadic nature. When degradation happens intermittently, pinpointing the source without historical evidence becomes almost impossible.”

Passing probes narrow the investigation; they do not close it. A snapshot of a healthy cluster may miss an earlier slowdown, and the absence of container failures does not establish that the application or its dependencies are performing well. The next step is to connect the user’s reported delay to measurements from the affected period.

Telemetry across the hybrid stack: Sifting signal from noise

Resolving sporadic slowness requires moving beyond surface-level Kubernetes metrics to continuous, multi-layer telemetry. Modern cloud-native architectures do not exist in isolation; a user request may depend on application code, container runtimes, virtualized or bare-metal infrastructure, and public cloud APIs. The relevant layers depend on the deployment.

“HPE OpsRamp collects signals continuously across every layer of the stack — Kubernetes nodes, pods, ingress controllers, and services — capturing logs, events, and metrics,” Ramachandran says. “The foundational step in troubleshooting sporadic issues is having a continuous record. You must go back into the telemetry history to correlate user-reported symptoms with actual signal evidence.”

“When degradation happens intermittently, pinpointing the source without historical evidence becomes almost impossible.”

However, Ramachandran emphasizes that finding the evidence within telemetry signals is rarely straightforward.

“It often requires intelligence to sift through the noise,” he says. “An anomaly might not appear as an obvious spike in a single metric. Instead, it might be a subtle variation or a correlated behavior where two separate signals both look normal individually, but their combined behavior produces latency.”

A practical investigation starts with the affected transaction and time window. Compare query response times and queries per second with pod health and counts, then look for variations in the collected signals that coincide with the slowdown.

A correlation identifies a candidate explanation; it does not prove the cause on its own. After making a change, compare the same user-facing measures with the earlier behavior to check whether performance improves. Because the scenario is composite, the team still needs to validate any suspected cause in its own environment.

“An anomaly might not appear as an obvious spike in a single metric. Instead, it might be a subtle variation or a correlated behavior where two separate signals both look normal individually, but their combined behavior produces latency.”

Coverage depends on the agents, integrations, permissions, and application instrumentation teams configure.

OpsRamp provides several ways to collect evidence across the relevant tiers:

  • Application: OpenTelemetry-compatible trace collection for instrumented applications. Teams must configure application instrumentation and the collection path; infrastructure monitoring alone does not generate application traces.
  • Orchestration: Kubernetes agents collect cluster and workload telemetry; additional monitoring configuration can provide visibility into components such as ingress controllers.
  • Virtualization and HCI: Integrations with VMware, Nutanix, and HPE Morpheus VM Essentials Software collect inventory and performance data to help investigate infrastructure bottlenecks.
  • Hardware: Redfish protocol integration for telemetry from supported physical servers, with the required API access and gateway connectivity.

Navigating black-box dependencies outside the cluster

Applications can depend on services outside their Kubernetes cluster, Ramachandran says. A user request might originate inside a private cluster but call an external SaaS endpoint, a database outside the mesh, or a public cloud AI model.

When an application relies on external third-party services, visibility hits a boundary. “If your application makes calls to a public AI model or an external web service, you enter a domain outside your direct monitoring control,” Ramachandran explains. “To rule out external dependencies as the source of slowness, you must quantify their performance as a black box.”

To bridge this visibility gap, teams can use synthetic transactions or other response-time measurements, Ramachandran says. Comparing those measurements with the affected application’s transactions helps assess whether an external dependency’s behavior coincides with the slowdown.

Teams still need to check that the measurements reflect the relevant request path and workload. Synthetic checks provide evidence at the service boundary; they do not reveal the provider’s internal root cause or automatically distinguish every external delay from an internal one. Teams should also identify who owns each dependency and who can investigate when access or instrumentation stops at that boundary.

Telemetry also needs security controls. In AI workloads, prompts, responses, and retrieved documents can appear in logs and traces. Teams should decide what to collect, where that information goes, and who can access it. Design cross-layer visibility alongside existing access and data-handling policies.

Alerting philosophy: From static dashboards to agentic copilots

As environments grow more complex, interpreting telemetry across multiple dashboards becomes difficult. Determining which metrics warrant a real-time alert versus passive monitoring is an ongoing operational challenge.

“Deciding which signals deserve an alert is where science and technology meet domain art,” Ramachandran says. “There is no magic formula. It requires encoding explicit and tacit human operational knowledge into the monitoring platform so the system understands what actually impacts user experience.”

Curated dashboards remain useful for predefined views of system behavior, while AI assistants offer another way to explore operational data. HPE OpsRamp Software includes an AI-powered operations copilot that lets operators explore complex telemetry through natural language.

HPE describes capabilities for investigating incidents, correlating evidence, and recommending next steps. Those capabilities depend on the data available to the platform and the features enabled in the customer’s deployment.

Looking ahead, Ramachandran sees an even more fundamental change in cloud-native operations. He frames machine-led interpretation as a direction for increasingly complex environments, with safeguards still needed before operational changes.

“We are rapidly approaching a point where the first responder to telemetry must be machine intelligence.”

“Today, human operators remain the primary first point of interpretation for telemetry,” Ramachandran tells TNS. “But as stack complexity increases with more moving parts and dynamic interactions, expecting a human to digest all these signals first becomes intractable. We are rapidly approaching a point where the first responder to telemetry must be machine intelligence.”

AI-assisted analysis and autonomous changes are separate operational decisions. Ramachandran cautions that AI outputs can be nondeterministic while IT operations often require repeatable behavior.

He recommends retaining human oversight and establishing reliable safeguards before allowing AI findings to trigger operational changes. Teams need to validate a diagnosis and confirm the effect of any response, even when an assistant helps assemble the evidence.

The foundation is instrumentation: Collect the necessary telemetry, establish workload-specific baselines and thresholds, and verify improvements against the user’s experience.

Green cluster indicators are a useful starting point, but application measurements determine whether the service delivers what users need.

Every pod is green, yet users still wait. HPE OpsRamp’s Mahesh Ramachandran explains how telemetry history exposes the slowdowns dashboards miss.

The post Your database decision could come back to haunt you appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
When building AI prototypes, developers naturally want to get up and running as fast as possible. But move too fast, and those decisions can come back to haunt you if they lead you to make flippant decisions about data infrastructure. 

For smaller, less-regulated startups building SaaS or internal applications, the consequences may not be as dire. Wherever you start building, you can usually keep running there even when applications move into production. 

But for large-scale enterprises operating in highly regulated environments — think healthcare, finance, government — some developer-friendly database platforms simply can’t meet the security, compliance, deployment, availability, and reliability requirements that emerge when it’s time to shift into production. 

Yes, you can re-platform. But it’ll cost you in redevelopment work, labor, and operational overhead. Choosing a database that can support both prototyping and production from Day 1 could let you skip those headaches altogether. 

The cost of choosing a database you’ll outgrow

Moving an application from one database platform to another as developers move prototypes into production may not seem like a particularly arduous transaction. After all, since nothing’s in production yet, there’s no real risk of downtime. That changes for teams that don’t discover the mismatch until after launch.

But the risks lie elsewhere, largely in wasted time and money — and they usually don’t reveal themselves until it’s too late to change course cheaply. 

When asked what happens when enterprises prototype on developer-friendly platforms without production-ready security, compliance, and deployment flexibility, Phillip Merrick, co-founder and CEO of pgEdge, tells The New Stack they may be looking at significant, costly rework: 

“You’ve got to look at retargeting the whole application to a new compliant platform, where it can run on-premises in a tightly managed cloud environment. And that’s going to require some amount of rework.”

“Choose the wrong platform, and you are going to incur additional costs.”

Besides the direct cost of technical work — which can get particularly gnarly if the application relies on proprietary capabilities from the original platform — Merrick cautions enterprises about the additional operational and administrative burdens of moving to and managing a new environment, including a second procurement cycle that few may plan for. It also takes time and resources to establish the necessary agentic operations strategy. 

Bottom line, he doesn’t see any way around the added expense: “Choose the wrong platform, and you are going to incur additional costs.”

  • Scaling AI Inference at the Edge With Distributed PostgreSQL
  • Why most AI projects fail: It’s infrastructure and people
  • Moving AI apps from prototype to production requires enterprise-grade postgres infrastructure
  • How Distributed Postgres Solves Cloud’s High-Availability Problem

Why teams don’t realize the problem until it’s too late

Many enterprises are drawn to fast, developer-friendly platforms because they’re snappy, easy to use, and often support agentic AI applications. That’s understandable. 

But Merrick tells The New Stack that too many developers default to these platforms without considering whether they match their enterprise’s specific production requirements — for example, whether they offer deployment choice. Security by default? High availability? 

In the end, that can leave a prototype stuck on infrastructure that just can’t support production in highly regulated industries. That’s because the prototyping platform and the production platform are often two different products, built by different teams for different buyers, not two tiers of the same thing. That’s because the prototyping platform and the production platform are often two different products, built by different teams for different buyers, not two tiers of the same thing.

“If you prototyped in an environment that doesn’t match up with your enterprise production requirements, then you have no choice but to re-platform.”

Being able to deploy in a tightly controlled cloud environment or on-premises, meet strict security and compliance requirements, and count on 99.99% uptime may not be an immediate priority for a small startup or less-regulated company. Still, it’s non-negotiable for many large enterprises. 

“If you prototyped in an environment that doesn’t match up with your enterprise production requirements, then you have no choice but to re-platform,” explains Merrick.

From where he sits, that infrastructure mismatch likely plays an outsized role in why so many generative AI and agentic prototypes never make it into production or, when they do, only produce scant business value. And at this point, the tale of underwhelming AI returns is an old line: MIT NANDA reports 95% of organizations are getting “zero return” on Generative AI investments. At the same time, IDC research with Lenovo says that for every 33 AI proofs-of-concept developed, only four make it into production.

What a database built for both stages looks like

While data infrastructure missteps aren’t solely responsible for AI projects failing to reach production, choosing the right database from Day 1 can remove one obstacle. 

Per Merrick, that means finding a platform that does away with the longstanding trade-off between developer speed and enterprise requirements: 

“If you’re an enterprise developer, there has been a trade-off: ‘If I want developer speed, am I willing to relax my enterprise requirements for this prototype, knowing that I’m going to have to incur the cost later to re-platform the [application] into my production environment?’”

Specifically, he says such a database platform needs enterprise-grade controls, deployment flexibility, high availability, and scalability — all on the same underlying platform. 

“It’s the comfort of knowing that it’s the same. If your application behaves one way on [the] cloud, it’s going to behave exactly the same way in your cloud or on-premises.”

That consistency is the kicker, as Merrick says it’s what gives developers the ability to move between environments without having to take on excessive rework. As he explains to The New Stack: “It’s the comfort of knowing that it’s the same. If your application behaves one way on [the] cloud, it’s going to behave exactly the same way in your cloud or on-premises.”

It’s possible to scale without re-platforming

pgEdge aims to give developers that continuity with pgEdge Starfleet, a new Postgres cloud database platform designed to bridge the gap between AI prototypes and production.

Merrick describes it to The New Stack as “the only 100% Postgres platform that combines a smooth developer experience and the AI tooling that developers want with the security, compliance, scalability, reliability, and deployment flexibility that the enterprise demands.” 

He also claims any developer can use it to get a database up and running in under two minutes, using the free 14-day trial to start building immediately and then deploy into different environments as production needs evolve. 

For smaller teams without strict requirements for deployment location or enterprise controls, that may simply mean going into production on pgEdge’s managed cloud, where developers can scale up instance sizes as needed. 

But what Merrick stresses as most important for larger enterprises is Starfleet’s ability to support other deployment models: “If, for your production environment, it needs to be your cloud, you can very easily migrate from Starfleet managed to Starfleet BYO Cloud.”

There’s also the option for on-premises deployment via a simple migration to pgEdge Enterprise Postgres, the company’s self-hosted option. “But it’s the very same Postgres platform you’re running on Starfleet,” he points out. “So it is not a re-platform. You’re just moving to a different underlying infrastructure. It’s the same Postgres on top.” 

This, he argues, is an important distinction, as some competing platforms use either only modified Postgres or Postgres-compatible databases. In contrast, pgEdge Starfleet allows developers to keep 100% standard Postgres across environments.

In BYO Cloud and on-premises deployments, Merrick adds that developers can go one step further to multi-master, multi-region Postgres for high availability and true zero-downtime maintenance, which he previously told The New Stack is the solution to the cloud’s high-availability problem. 

“So starting with a free trial and then a credit card and going all the way up to globally distributed, multi-region, multi-active Postgres clusters,” he says, “that is a scaling path that nobody else can deliver.”

And you can keep developer speed, too

Meeting enterprise requirements for deployment, security, and availability can come at the expense of developer convenience during prototyping. But Merrick believes developers shouldn’t have to accept this tradeoff. 

“You can have that developer speed. You can have those enterprise requirements. Bingo, that’s what pgEdge Starfleet is all about,” he says.

One way the platform supports speed is by providing tools to reduce the work developers need to do themselves. The pgEdge Agentic AI Toolkit, which includes an MCP server, a RAG API server, and the pgEdge Vectorizer extension, connects coding agents to Postgres, supports RAG applications, and automatically creates and maintains vector embeddings. 

The other advantage Merrick points to is true copy-on-write database branching.

“As a developer, you are going to want to have the ability to work against a copy of your production data,” Merrick tells The New Stack, whether that be to support parallel agentic AI experiments or tackle production debugging.

By creating a logical copy of the whole database and only writing new data when changes are made, copy-on-write branching means developers don’t have to duplicate the existing database for every experiment. This way, developers can spin up isolated database branches for testing or debugging without exposing sensitive data, dealing with long copy times, or consuming excessive disk storage.

“Copy-on-write branching is incredibly powerful. Most Postgres vendors do not implement it,” says Merrick.

To be fair, he adds that Neon popularized the approach years ago. But he also tells The New Stack that doing so required completely rewriting the Postgres storage engine, thereby making the resulting platform no longer 100% standard Postgres.

And thus, we are back to the original trade-off: Do developers have to choose between developer speed and production-grade infrastructure? 

Merrick says no: “Our innovation is being able to deliver copy-on-write database branching without having to change Postgres at all.” Xata, another Postgres platform, also markets copy-on-write branching on unmodified Postgres.

For developers, it looks like having the best of both worlds.
